lists.text:
1. Launch a citywide campaign on meal planning and proper food storage.
2. Provide households with refrigerator thermometers and storage guides.
3. Teach residents how to distinguish “best before” dates from food safety deadlines.
4. Offer cooking classes focused on using leftovers.
5. Create an online recipe hub for common surplus ingredients.
6. Introduce food-waste prevention lessons in local schools.
7. Help school cafeterias adjust meal portions based on student feedback.
8. Install share tables where students can leave unopened, unwanted food.
9. Allow students to choose side dishes rather than taking mandatory servings.
10. Give restaurants tools to track and analyze kitchen waste.
11. Encourage restaurants to offer multiple portion sizes.
12. Provide reusable or recyclable containers for restaurant leftovers.
13. Connect restaurants with apps that sell surplus meals at a discount.
14. Recognize businesses that meet measurable food-waste reduction targets.
15. Help grocery stores improve demand forecasting and inventory management.
16. Promote discounted “eat soon” shelves for products nearing their quality dates.
17. Encourage stores to sell cosmetically imperfect produce.
18. Expand sales of loose produce so shoppers can buy only what they need.
19. Support refill shops that let customers purchase small quantities of staples.
20. Create a citywide food-rescue hotline for businesses with surplus food.
21. Fund refrigerated vehicles for transporting donated food safely.
22. Install shared cold-storage facilities for food banks and pantries.
23. Coordinate regular pickups of surplus food from grocery stores.
24. Recruit volunteers to deliver recovered food to community organizations.
25. Publish a directory of organizations that accept different kinds of food donations.
26. Offer businesses training on safe food donation procedures.
27. Create a grant program for food-rescue equipment and operating costs.
28. Partner with caterers to donate safe, untouched food from events.
29. Encourage event organizers to require accurate meal RSVPs.
30. Add food-donation plans to permits for large public events.
31. Establish community fridges with clear safety and maintenance rules.
32. Support neighborhood food-sharing networks.
33. Organize gleaning teams to collect unharvested crops from nearby farms.
34. Connect backyard fruit-tree owners with volunteers who can harvest excess produce.
35. Create a produce market for surplus crops from local farms.
36. Help farmers access buyers for products that do not meet cosmetic standards.
37. Support food processors that turn surplus produce into soups, sauces, or preserves.
38. Encourage breweries and bakeries to use surplus bread or grain in new products.
39. Help food businesses identify safe opportunities to use byproducts as animal feed.
40. Introduce smaller package options in municipal food purchasing contracts.
41. Require city-run facilities to measure and report food waste.
42. Adjust meal orders at city facilities using historical consumption data.
43. Conduct a citywide food-waste audit to identify the largest sources.
44. Set a public food-waste reduction target and report progress annually.
45. Create a business network for sharing surplus ingredients and prevention practices.
46. Offer technical assistance to apartment buildings for food-waste prevention and separation.
47. Provide curbside collection of unavoidable food scraps for composting.
48. Establish community composting sites in neighborhoods without curbside service.
49. Expand anaerobic digestion capacity for food scraps that cannot be eaten or donated.
50. Design waste-collection fees that reward businesses for reducing discarded food.

50. Send remaining suitable food scraps to anaerobic digestion facilities that produce renewable energy.
